prompt: What does the octet rule say?

choices.text: Atoms tend to gain or lose electrons until they have eight electrons in their valence shell.
Atoms tend to gain or lose electrons until they have eight electrons in total.
choices.why: The rule counts only the electrons in the valence shell. An Mg^2+ ion, for example, has 10 electrons in all but eight in its valence shell.

choices.text: Atoms always gain electrons until their valence shell holds eight electrons.
choices.why: Metal atoms such as sodium reach an octet by losing electrons, not by gaining them.

choices.text: Atoms tend to combine in groups of eight to form stable compounds.
choices.why: The rule is about the number of electrons in an atom's valence shell, not the number of atoms in a compound.

explanation: Eight electrons in the valence shell is a particularly stable arrangement, and the tendency of atoms to reach it is called the octet rule. Nonmetal atoms reach an octet by gaining electrons; metal atoms reach one by losing their valence electrons.

prompt: Which statement about the octet rule is accurate?

choices.text: It is a very good rule of thumb, but not all atoms satisfy it at all times.
It is a strict law: no atom or ion can ever exist without an octet.
choices.why: A sodium atom has only one valence electron, yet it is stable in elemental form. The octet rule is a rule of thumb, not a strict law.

choices.text: It applies only to the noble gases, which already have eight valence electrons.
choices.why: The rule describes the tendency of other atoms to gain or lose electrons until they have eight, which explains why they form the ions they do.

choices.text: It applies only to elements in the second row of the periodic table.
choices.why: Atoms in other rows follow it too; a chlorine atom, in the third row, completes an octet in its n = 3 shell when it forms Cl^−.

explanation: The octet rule is not always satisfied for all atoms at all times, and it is not impossible to violate. Even so, it is a very good rule of thumb for understanding the bonding arrangements atoms make and why atoms form the ions they do.

prompt: In chemical reactions, sodium forms Na^+ ions but not Na^2+ ions. Why does sodium stop at a 1+ charge?

choices.text: Removing a second electron takes much more energy than chemical reactions normally supply.
An Na^2+ ion cannot be made, no matter how much energy is supplied.
choices.why: Na^2+ can be made by adding even more energy; ordinary chemical reactions just don't supply that much.

choices.text: A sodium atom has only one electron, so there is none left to remove.
choices.why: A sodium atom has 11 electrons. Only one is a valence electron, and the Na^+ ion still has 10.

choices.text: Losing a second electron would give the ion an octet it does not yet have.
choices.why: Na^+ already has a complete octet, so losing another electron can't be what gives it one.

explanation: Removing sodium's one valence electron takes little energy and leaves Na^+ with a complete octet. Taking away another electron would require much more energy than is normally available in chemical reactions, so sodium stops at a 1+ charge.

prompt: Which of these species has a complete octet in its valence shell?

choices.text: Cs^+

choices.why: An oxygen atom has six valence electrons, so O^− has seven. Oxygen must gain two electrons, becoming O^2−, to complete its octet.

choices.text: Mg^+
choices.why: Mg^+ still has one electron in its n = 3 shell. Magnesium must lose both valence electrons before its full n = 2 shell becomes the valence shell.

choices.text: Al^+
choices.why: Al^+ still has two electrons in its n = 3 shell. Aluminum must lose all three valence electrons to be left with an octet.

explanation: A cesium atom ([Xe]6s^1) loses its single valence electron, so in Cs^+ the full n = 5 shell (5s^2 5p^6) becomes the valence shell, with eight electrons. Each of the other species has gained or lost too few electrons to reach an octet.

prompt: A potassium atom, [Ar]4s^1, transfers its valence electron to a nonmetal atom. What is the electron configuration of the K^+ ion that forms?

choices.text: [Ar]

choices.why: That is the configuration of the neutral K atom. The K^+ ion has lost its 4s electron.
Adding an electron would make K^−. A metal atom such as potassium loses its valence electron instead.
That is what would be left after removing two electrons. K^+ has lost only one, so it keeps a complete octet in its n = 3 shell.

explanation: Losing its single 4s electron leaves K^+ with the configuration [Ar], which has eight electrons in the n = 3 shell. The ion satisfies the octet rule, just as Na^+ ([Ne]) does.

prompt: When a sodium atom meets a chlorine atom, one electron moves from the Na atom to the Cl atom. How does the octet rule account for this transfer?

choices.text: Afterward, the Na^+ ion and the Cl^− ion both have complete octets.
Afterward, the Cl^− ion has a complete octet, but the Na^+ ion has none.
choices.why: Na^+ has an octet too. With its 3s electron gone, its n = 2 shell, which holds eight electrons, is now the valence shell.

choices.text: Afterward, sodium has an octet, but chlorine has only seven valence electrons.
choices.why: Chlorine starts with seven valence electrons and gains one, so Cl^− has eight.

choices.text: Afterward, the Na^+ ion and the Cl^− ion have equal numbers of electrons.
choices.why: Na^+ has 10 electrons and Cl^− has 18. What the two ions share is eight electrons in the valence shell.

explanation: To obtain an octet, a sodium atom ([Ne]3s^1) must lose an electron and a chlorine atom ([Ne]3s^2 3p^5) must gain one. Transferring one electron does both, so Na^+ ([Ne]) and Cl^− ([Ne]3s^2 3p^6) each end up with a complete, energetically stable octet.

prompt: A potassium atom transfers its valence electron to an iodine atom, and the product is KI. What is the ionic bond in KI?

choices.text: The attraction between the oppositely charged K^+ and I^− ions
The electron that moved from the K atom to the I atom
choices.why: The transfer produces the ions, but the bond itself is the attraction between them once they have opposite charges.

choices.text: A pair of electrons shared between the K and I atoms
choices.why: Here the electron is transferred completely, not shared. KI is held together by the attraction between its ions.

choices.text: The attraction between the K^+ ion and the electron it gave up
choices.why: That electron now belongs to the I^− ion. The bond is the attraction between the two ions, K^+ and I^−.

explanation: The attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. The electron transfer creates K^+ and I^−, and because opposite charges attract, the two ions are held together as KI.

prompt: A rubidium atom and a bromine atom react. Which describes the electron transfer between them?

choices.text: One electron moves from Rb to Br, forming Rb^+ and Br^−.
One electron moves from Br to Rb, forming Rb^− and Br^+.
choices.why: Rubidium is a metal with one valence electron, which it loses; bromine, with seven valence electrons, gains one.

choices.text: Two electrons move from Rb to Br, forming Rb^2+ and Br^2−.
choices.why: Rubidium has only one valence electron to give, and bromine needs only one more electron to complete its octet.

choices.text: One electron moves from Rb to Br, forming Rb^− and Br^+.
choices.why: An atom that loses an electron becomes positive, and an atom that gains one becomes negative, so the ions are Rb^+ and Br^−.

explanation: Rubidium ([Kr]5s^1) reaches an octet by losing its one valence electron, and bromine (seven valence electrons) reaches one by gaining an electron. One electron moves from Rb to Br, giving Rb^+ and Br^−, which attract each other to form RbBr.

prompt: Which pair of elements would combine by transferring electrons to form an ionic bond?

choices.text: calcium and bromine
sodium and magnesium
choices.why: Both are metals, which tend to lose electrons. With no atom to accept them, no anion forms, and an ionic compound needs both a cation and an anion.

choices.text: chlorine and oxygen
choices.why: Both are nonmetals, which tend to gain electrons. Neither gives up electrons to form a cation, so no ionic bond forms between them.

choices.text: argon and potassium
choices.why: Argon already has a complete octet, so it does not accept potassium's electron. Potassium needs a nonmetal partner that gains electrons.

explanation: An ionic bond forms when metal atoms transfer electrons to nonmetal atoms and the resulting cations and anions attract. Calcium, a metal, loses electrons to bromine, a nonmetal, forming Ca^2+ and Br^− ions.

prompt: When metal atoms transfer electrons to nonmetal atoms to form an ionic compound, which statement must be true?

choices.text: Total electrons lost by the metal atoms equal total electrons gained by the nonmetal atoms.
The number of metal atoms equals the number of nonmetal atoms.
choices.why: The atoms needn't match in number. Magnesium fluoride, MgF2, has two F atoms for each Mg atom.

choices.text: Each metal atom loses exactly one electron to a nonmetal atom.
choices.why: Many metal atoms lose more than one electron; a magnesium atom, for example, loses two.

choices.text: Each nonmetal atom gains as many electrons as each metal atom loses.
choices.why: Only the totals must match. In MgF2 the Mg atom loses two electrons, while each F atom gains one.

explanation: Electrons are not created or destroyed in the transfer, so every electron a metal atom loses is gained by a nonmetal atom. This requirement is what sets the ratio of cations to anions in an ionic compound.

prompt: Metal atoms transfer electrons to nonmetal atoms, and the resulting ions attract one another. What is the overall charge of the ionic compound that forms?

choices.text: Zero, because the total positive charge equals the total negative charge
Positive, because the metal atoms have lost electrons
choices.why: The cations' positive charge is exactly balanced by the anions' negative charge, so the compound has no overall charge.

choices.text: Negative, because the nonmetal atoms have gained electrons
choices.why: The anions' negative charge is exactly balanced by the cations' positive charge, so the compound has no overall charge.

choices.text: It depends on which ion has the larger charge
choices.why: The ions combine in whatever ratio balances the charges, so the compound is neutral no matter what the individual charges are.

explanation: The ions combine in a ratio that makes the total positive charge equal the total negative charge, so the ionic compound is neutral overall. MgF2, for example, has two F^− ions for each Mg^2+ ion.

prompt: Aluminum atoms transfer electrons to fluorine atoms to form an ionic compound. What is its formula?

choices.text: AlF3
AlF
choices.why: An Al atom loses three electrons, but one F atom can accept only one. Three F atoms are needed.

choices.text: Al3F
choices.why: This has the ratio upside down: three Al atoms would lose nine electrons, but one F atom gains only one.

choices.text: AlF2
choices.why: Fluorine exists as F2 molecules, but that doesn't set the formula. Aluminum's three electrons go to three F atoms, one each.

explanation: An aluminum atom loses its three valence electrons to form Al^3+, and each fluorine atom gains one electron to form F^−. Three F atoms are needed to accept the three electrons, so the formula is AlF3.

prompt: A student describes the reaction of magnesium with nitrogen this way: "One Mg atom gives its two valence electrons to one N atom, so the formula is MgN." What is the mistake?

choices.text: An N atom needs three electrons, so three Mg atoms must serve two N atoms: Mg3N2.
Magnesium should take electrons from nitrogen, since N has more valence electrons.
choices.why: Metal atoms lose electrons and nonmetal atoms gain them. Mg loses its two valence electrons; N gains electrons.

choices.text: Each Mg atom should give three electrons, so the formula MgN is still right.
choices.why: Mg has only two valence electrons and forms Mg^2+; removing a third would break into the octet beneath.

choices.text: There is no mistake, because both ions now have complete octets.
choices.why: N has five valence electrons; with only two more it has seven, not eight. It needs three.

explanation: Each Mg atom loses 2 electrons and each N atom must gain 3, so electrons lost and gained balance only at 6: three Mg atoms lose 6 electrons and two N atoms gain 6. The formula is Mg3N2.

prompt: Magnesium atoms transfer electrons to sulfur atoms. How is the final formula of the ionic compound written?

choices.text: MgS

choices.why: By convention, the final formula of an ionic compound is written without the charges on the ions.

choices.text: Mg2S2
choices.why: One Mg atom's two electrons complete one S atom's octet, so one of each is enough. Formulas use the lowest ratio.

choices.text: Mg2S
choices.why: Two Mg atoms would lose four electrons, but one S atom gains only two.

explanation: Each Mg atom loses two electrons and each S atom gains two, so one of each balances. The final formula is written without the charges: MgS.

prompt: A student looks at the formula Na2S and says, "The 2 means each sodium atom gave two electrons to the sulfur atom." What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: The 2 counts Na atoms: each gives one electron, and two supply the two electrons S needs.
Nothing; each Na atom does give two electrons, which the 2 records.
choices.why: A sodium atom has only one valence electron, and it forms Na^+, not Na^2+.

choices.text: The 2 means the S atom gained two electrons from each Na atom.
choices.why: That would be four electrons. A sulfur atom needs only two more to complete its octet.

choices.text: The 2 is the overall charge on the compound, which is 2−.
choices.why: Subscripts in a formula count atoms or ions, so the 2 tells how many Na atoms there are.

explanation: Each Na atom loses its single valence electron, while an S atom must gain two to complete its octet. Two Na atoms are needed to supply those two electrons, and the subscript 2 records that count.

prompt: Each formula below is proposed for an ionic compound made by electron transfer between the atoms shown. Which formula cannot be right?

choices.text: MgCl
CsBr
choices.why: A Cs atom loses one electron and a Br atom gains one, so one of each balances. CsBr is a possible formula.

choices.text: K2O
choices.why: Two K atoms each lose one electron, giving the two electrons an O atom gains. K2O is a possible formula.

choices.text: CaO
choices.why: A Ca atom loses two electrons and an O atom gains two, so one of each balances. CaO is a possible formula.

explanation: A Mg atom loses two electrons, but a Cl atom gains only one, so in MgCl the electrons lost would not equal the electrons gained. Two Cl atoms are needed, so the formula must be MgCl2.

prompt: The strength of an ionic bond depends mainly on which two characteristics of the ions?

choices.text: The magnitude of their charges and their size
Their masses and the number of ions in the formula
choices.why: Neither mass nor the number of ions sets the bond strength; the magnitude of the charges and the size of the ions do.

choices.text: The magnitude of their charges and their masses
choices.why: Charge is one factor, but the other is size, not mass: the smaller the ions, the stronger the ionic bond.

choices.text: Their size and the total number of electrons they contain
choices.why: Size is one factor; the other is the magnitude of the charges. The total electron count isn't what sets bond strength.

explanation: The greater the magnitude of the charges, the stronger the ionic bond. The smaller the ions, the stronger the bond too, because smaller ions can get closer together.

prompt: What does the lattice energy of an ionic compound measure?

choices.text: The strength of the ionic bonding in the compound
The energy needed to remove an electron from a gas-phase atom
choices.why: That is ionization energy, a property of a single atom, not of an ionic compound.

choices.text: The energy change when a gas-phase atom accepts an electron
choices.why: That is electron affinity, a property of a single atom, not of an ionic compound.

choices.text: The number of electrons transferred per formula unit
choices.why: Lattice energy is an energy, measured in kJ/mol, not a count of electrons.

explanation: Lattice energy is the measured strength of ionic bonding, given in kJ/mol. A compound with stronger ionic bonding, such as one with highly charged or small ions, has a larger lattice energy.

prompt: Which compound has the stronger ionic bonding, CaO or KBr?

choices.text: CaO, because its ions carry charges of larger magnitude
KBr, because its ions carry charges of smaller magnitude
choices.why: Smaller charges make a weaker ionic bond: the greater the magnitude of the charges, the stronger the bond.

choices.text: Neither; each has one cation per anion, so the bonds are equally strong
choices.why: A 1:1 ratio doesn't make the bonds equally strong. Ca^2+ and O^2− carry twice the charge of K^+ and Br^−.

choices.text: Neither can be predicted without measuring the lattice energies
choices.why: The charges are enough to predict it: the greater the magnitude of the charges, the stronger the ionic bond.

explanation: Ca^2+ and O^2− have charges of magnitude 2, while K^+ and Br^− have charges of magnitude 1. The greater the magnitude of the charges, the stronger the ionic bond, so CaO has the stronger bonding (its ions are also smaller, which strengthens it further).

prompt: Lattice energies (in kJ/mol): LiF 1,036; LiCl 853; NaCl 786; NaBr 747; MgF2 2,957. Which pair of these compounds shows the effect of cation size alone?

choices.text: LiCl and NaCl
LiF and LiCl
choices.why: These share the same cation, Li^+; only the anion changes, so this pair shows the effect of anion size.

choices.text: NaCl and NaBr
choices.why: Here the cation stays Na^+ and the anion changes from Cl^− to Br^−, so this pair shows the effect of anion size.

choices.text: LiF and MgF2
choices.why: The cation changes charge as well as identity (Li^+ to Mg^2+), so this pair mixes the effects of charge and size.

explanation: LiCl and NaCl have the same anion, Cl^−, and cations with the same 1+ charge; only the cation's size differs. Li^+ is smaller than Na^+ (Li is higher in the same column), so LiCl has the larger lattice energy, 853 versus 786 kJ/mol.

prompt: Lattice energies (in kJ/mol): Na2O 2,481; MgF2 2,957; MgO 3,791. Which best explains why MgO's value is the largest?

choices.text: Both of its ions have a charge of magnitude 2.
It has the most ions per formula unit.
choices.why: MgO has only two ions per formula unit; Na2O and MgF2 each have three.

choices.text: It has the most electrons transferred per formula unit.
choices.why: Each of the three compounds involves two electrons transferred per formula unit, so this can't explain the difference.

choices.text: Its ions are larger than those of the other two.
choices.why: Larger ions would make the bond weaker, not stronger. The difference comes from charge: in Na2O and MgF2, one of the ions has a charge of only 1.

explanation: In Na2O only the oxide ion has a 2− charge, and in MgF2 only the magnesium ion has a 2+ charge; in MgO both ions carry charges of magnitude 2. The greater the magnitude of the charges, the stronger the ionic bond, so MgO has the largest lattice energy.

prompt: Rank NaF, NaCl, and NaI from weakest to strongest ionic bonding.

choices.text: NaI < NaCl < NaF
NaF < NaCl < NaI
choices.why: This makes the compound with the largest anion the strongest. Smaller ions make stronger ionic bonds, so the order runs the other way.

choices.text: NaCl < NaF < NaI
choices.why: Nothing makes NaCl the weakest. The halide ions grow larger down the column (F^−, Cl^−, I^−), so bonding weakens steadily from NaF to NaI.

choices.text: All three are equal, because every ion has a charge of 1
choices.why: Equal charges remove one factor, but the anions still differ in size; the smaller the anion, the stronger the bond.

explanation: All three compounds have ions with charges of magnitude 1, so size decides. Going down the column from F to Cl to I the anions get larger, and larger ions can't get as close together, so the bonding weakens: NaI < NaCl < NaF.

prompt: A student predicts that CsCl has stronger ionic bonding than NaCl because "a cesium ion is bigger than a sodium ion, and bigger ions attract more strongly." What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: Smaller ions can get closer together, so the smaller Na^+ gives NaCl stronger bonding.
Nothing; a larger ion carries more charge, so CsCl has stronger bonding.
choices.why: Cs^+ and Na^+ both have a 1+ charge; being larger doesn't give an ion more charge.

choices.text: The prediction is right, but it is cesium's greater mass that makes CsCl stronger.
choices.why: Mass doesn't set bond strength, and CsCl isn't stronger: its larger Cs^+ ion makes its bonding weaker.

choices.text: Ion size has no effect on bond strength; only the charges matter.
choices.why: Size matters too: the smaller the ion, the stronger the ionic bond. With equal charges here, size decides.

explanation: Na^+ and Cs^+ both have a 1+ charge, but Cs is farther down the same column, so Cs^+ is the larger ion. Smaller ions can get closer together, so NaCl has the stronger ionic bonding; the student has the size effect backward.

prompt: Salt supplies Na^+ and Cl^− ions that the body needs. Endurance athletes can end up with dangerously low salt levels in their bodies. What is the usual cause?

choices.text: Drinking too much water, which dilutes the body's salt
Eating too little salt in their everyday diet
choices.why: Low salt in the body usually comes not from eating too little salt but from drinking so much water that the body's salt is diluted.

choices.text: Eating too much salt, which raises blood pressure
choices.why: Too much salt is linked to high blood pressure, not to low salt levels; low salt usually comes from drinking too much water.

choices.text: Salt breaking down into sodium metal and chlorine gas
choices.why: Salt does not turn back into its hazardous elements in the body; low salt levels come from dilution by too much water.

explanation: People with dangerously low salt levels usually haven't eaten too little salt; they have drunk so much water that the body's salt is diluted. That is why endurance athletes need to watch their water intake.

prompt: A strontium atom has the electron configuration [Kr]5s^2. How many electrons does it lose when it forms the ion predicted by the octet rule?
explanation: Strontium loses both 5s electrons to become Sr^2+. Its n = 4 shell (4s^2 4p^6), with eight electrons, then becomes the valence shell, satisfying the octet rule.

prompt: A selenium atom has the valence electron configuration 4s^2 4p^4. How many electrons does it gain when it forms the ion predicted by the octet rule?
explanation: Selenium has six valence electrons (2 + 4), so it gains two to complete an octet, 4s^2 4p^6, and becomes Se^2−.

prompt: Sodium reacts with phosphorus to form the ionic compound sodium phosphide. How many sodium atoms are needed to supply the electrons that one phosphorus atom gains?
explanation: A phosphorus atom has five valence electrons, so it gains three to complete its octet, but each sodium atom has only one valence electron to give. Three Na atoms are needed for each P atom, giving Na3P.

prompt: Aluminum atoms transfer electrons to oxygen atoms to form aluminum oxide. How many electrons in total are transferred to make one formula unit?
explanation: Each Al atom loses 3 electrons and each O atom gains 2. The smallest number both 3 and 2 divide into is 6, so two Al atoms lose 6 electrons and three O atoms gain 6, giving Al2O3.

prompt: Six barium atoms transfer all of their valence electrons to iodine atoms. How many iodide ions form?
explanation: Each Ba atom loses its two valence electrons, so six Ba atoms give up 12 electrons. Each I atom gains just one electron to complete its octet, so 12 I^− ions form (six formula units of BaI2).

prompt: Sodium's electron configuration is 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1. If two electrons were removed from a sodium atom to make an Na^2+ ion, how many electrons would be left in its n = 2 shell?
explanation: The first electron removed is the 3s electron, which leaves Na^+ with its n = 2 octet (2s^2 2p^6) intact. The second must come from the n = 2 shell itself, leaving seven electrons there, so Na^2+ would no longer have an octet.
